newsitem.title: JAPAN: Prosecutors say DKB raids connected to Nomura case.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutors say DKB raids connected to Nomura case.

text.p: Officials of the Tokyo Public Prosecutors' Office said on Tuesday they had raided Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) in connection with their investigation into a scandal at Nomura Securities Co Ltd.
Deputy Chief Prosecutor Kunihiro Matsuo said prosecutors were investigating DKB in connection with the alleged violation of the commercial code by Nomura.
He said prosecutors raided several locations including DKB's headquarters and the homes of several bank officials.
About 200 investigators were involved. He said: "I cannot make any further announcement as the investigation is still under way."

DKB, the world's third biggest bank in terms of assets, said earlier that it regretted the raids, but stayed silent over reports that it provided questionable loans to the racketeer at the centre of the Nomura Securities payoff scandal, Ryuichi Koike.

"We find it extremely regrettable that we have brought on ourselves a situation in which Tokyo prosecutors have searched (our offices). We will cooperate fully with investigations," a bank spokesman said.
He declined to comment on DKB's reported link with Koike.
"We do not comment on deals with our individual customers," the spokesman said.
Koike and his younger brother Yoshinori Koike were arrested last week on suspicion of taking some 50 million yen ($438,000) in illegal payments from Nomura.
Two former Nomura executives and a third senior Nomura official have also been arrested in the case.
Japan's Commercial Code bans companies from making payments to "sokaiya", racketeers who extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt shareholder meetings.
After the Nomura payoff scandal emerged in early March, media reports said DKB had loaned three billion yen ($26.3 million) in 1989 to the younger Koike's real estate firm.
The elder Koike reportedly used the money to buy 300,000 shares in each of the nation's top four brokerages, including Nomura, and put up the shares as collateral for DKB loans.
On Tuesday, the Yomiuri Shimbun daily said that DKB had provided questionable loans worth some 600 million yen ($5.26 million) in 1994 without collateral to Ryuichi Koike.
This was reported to be the latest chunk of a total of 30 billion yen ($263 million) in loans extended to Koike by DKB and a closely linked financial firm, Daiwa Shinyo.
DKB is still holding unrecoverable problem loans worth 7.5 billion yen ($65.7 million) and Daiwa Shinyo 1.2 billion yen ($10.5 million) from such loans, Japanese media reported.
The Yomiuri said prosecutors were particularly looking at whether the latest uncollateralised loans to Koike had violated the Commercial Code and involved breach of trust.
